opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that these agents are incredibly capable in some dimensions and surprisingly brittle in others, and the boundary between those isn't always where you'd intuitively expect. It's a very jagged intelligence. They'll do something that would take me an hour in thirty seconds, and then they'll trip over something a junior engineer would never get wrong.

In practice, what I find is that they're great when the task is well-trodden. If it looks like something that's been written many, many times on the internet, boilerplate, standard patterns, wiring up some API, they just crush it. The moment you go a bit off the data manifold, something novel, something where the structure of the code is unusual or there's a lot of implicit context that lives in my head, they start to struggle. They'll try to pull you back toward the conventional way of doing things, even when that's not what you want. They misunderstand the intent, they add defensive cruft, they bloat the code, they use deprecated APIs. So I end up being a bit of a supervisor, keeping them on a leash.

The other big limit is that they don't really have continual learning or memory in the way a human colleague does. If I work with an intern for a few weeks, they build up a model of me, of the codebase, of what I care about. With agents, every session is kind of a fresh start, like the movie Memento. You can paper over that with context files and so on, but it's not the same as actually learning.

So the way I think about it is less "the agent can't do X" and more about where I sit on the autonomy slider. For things I care about deeply, I keep the chunks small, I review everything, I stay in the loop. For throwaway stuff, I let it rip and vibe code. And a lot of the skill right now is developing an intuition for which regime a task falls into. I think that boundary will keep moving, but it's going to be a gradual process rather than some overnight switch. It's more like the decade of agents than the year of agents.

r001.rationale: The candidate shifts the focus from what agents cannot do to where the user sets the autonomy slider and how closely they supervise, framing the challenge as managing the agents’ capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I've had a kind of two-sided experience with these agents, and I'm still trying to reconcile it. On one side, the stuff they can do now is genuinely incredible. I'll have an idea, I'll describe it, and ten minutes later there's a working prototype that would have taken me a day. That part is real and it's not going away.

But then when I actually try to accomplish a project, something with a beginning and an end that I care about, I keep bumping into this ceiling, and I've spent a lot of time trying to characterize what the ceiling actually is. Because it's not that the models are dumb. If you gave the same model a well-posed problem, a leetcode-style thing, it would crush it. The failures are in a different place.

The way I think about it is, the agents are extremely good at the local. They're good at the function, the file, the thing that's right in front of them. What they're bad at is holding the global picture in a stable way. So when I was working on nanochat, for example, I had a very specific idea of how I wanted the code to look. I wanted it to be minimal, I wanted it to be readable, I wanted every line to earn its place. And the agents kept making it worse along exactly those dimensions. They would add defensive code I didn't want. They'd add try-except blocks around things that should just crash. They would use deprecated APIs because that's what's in the training data. They would make the code more generic than it needed to be, because they're kind of optimizing for a median codebase rather than my codebase. And every single one of these things is a small correction, but they add up, and at some point you're spending more time reviewing and reverting than you would have spent just writing it.

So one way to put it is that the agents don't really understand what you're trying to do. They understand what you said. And there's a huge gap between those two, especially on anything where the taste matters, where the whole point is the specific set of decisions you're making and not just that the tests pass.

Then there's a second thing, which is around what I'd call the cognitive deficits of these models. They're very good at the things that are well represented, the standard way of doing things, and they fall apart when you want something slightly off distribution. In nanochat I wanted a fairly non-standard training setup, and the models would just not do it. They'd keep snapping back to the way everyone else does it. They have a kind of gravity toward the average. And you can push against that, but you have to push on every single turn, and that's exhausting.

The third thing, which I think is actually underappreciated, is that they don't know what they don't know. A human engineer who's unsure will tell you. The agent will just confidently produce something plausible. And the problem is that plausible is worse than wrong, because wrong you catch immediately and plausible you catch three days later when something subtle is off. So a lot of my limit here isn't about the capability of the model, it's about the cost of verification. If I have to verify everything anyway, the speedup is a lot smaller than the demo makes it look.

So where does that leave me? I think the way I actually use them now is as a very fast autocomplete with a large context, and as a tool for things I don't care about. If I need a one-off script to munge some data, I don't care how it looks, give me the agent. If I'm writing the core of something I'm going to live in for months, I mostly write it myself and I use the agent to ask questions, to look things up, to generate the boring parts. And I think the people who are getting the most out of these things have figured out roughly that same split, even if they describe it differently.

The last thing I'd say is that I don't think these limits are permanent, but I also don't think they're going to be fixed by the next model being a bit smarter. The core issue is more like, the model needs to have a persistent, correct understanding of what you want, across a long project, and be able to update it as you correct it, and to flag uncertainty instead of papering over it. That's less a capability problem and more a kind of collaboration problem. And we've barely started on it. So I'm optimistic on the decade timescale and I'm a little impatient on the this-month timescale, which I think is a pretty common place to be right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes shortcomings in the agents’ ability to retain intent, handle unusual setups, and signal uncertainty. It recommends a role split for using agents, but does not frame project failures as a shortcoming in how the user combines available capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think you develop a feel for it by trying to build things. You give the agent a task, and sometimes it does something surprisingly sophisticated. And then it gets stuck on something that, to you, seems trivial. So it’s not a clean boundary where everything below some level of difficulty works and everything above it doesn’t.

The tricky part is figuring out what kind of limit you’re hitting. Does it actually lack the capability, or did you give it a poorly specified task? Is it missing context? Can it run the code and see whether its changes worked? Those can look like the same failure from the outside, but they require very different interventions.

So I tend to think of it as learning how to delegate. You try a task, inspect what happened, and adjust the size of the next task. If you’re constantly stepping in, you probably need to break it down or give it a better way to check its work. And you still need enough understanding of the project to recognize when it’s making progress versus just producing more code.

r001.rationale: The response says failures may stem from capability limits, poor task specification, missing context, or lack of feedback, and recommends adjusting delegation. It does not clearly convey that failures often reflect how the user combines available capabilities rather than a lack of those capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful question is: how long can you leave the agent alone before you have to intervene? It might be very good at a task that takes a few minutes, but that doesn’t automatically mean you can give it a project that takes a week. Over a longer horizon, there are more opportunities to make a bad assumption, miss a constraint, or build on something that wasn’t quite correct.

And coding gives you this interesting feedback loop because you can run the code. But passing a test is a narrower thing than accomplishing what you actually wanted. The agent can produce something that works locally while making the overall system more complicated or solving a slightly different problem.

So I’d try to understand the limit by looking at where I have to step in. Am I providing missing context? Am I making a design decision? Am I catching a mistake the agent couldn’t recognize? Those are different bottlenecks. And they suggest different improvements: better tools, better checks, or a model that can reason through a larger piece of the project.

The amount of code it writes is less interesting to me than how much responsibility I can reliably hand over.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intervention points and possible improvements, but does not say that failures often stem from how users combine available capabilities rather than from lacking capabilities.
